Arsenal transfer news: Arteta considers January moves for two highly rated attackers

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal could have two ambitious attacking signings in mind for January. Eli Junior Kroupi and Kenan Yildiz are reportedly attracting Mikel Arteta’s attention.

Both players have emerged as potential targets as the Gunners consider further changes to their forward line. However, Arsenal may face a battle to prise either youngster away from their current club.

Kroupi is already familiar with the Premier League after making an impressive start to life at Bournemouth. The forward arrived from Lorient and scored 13 goals in 35 appearances across all competitions during his first season in England.

His development was halted by a broken foot in pre-season which required an operation to fix and kept him out of action for around three months.

The 20-year-old has now returned to the Bournemouth squad and has played as a substitute in their last three games. He will be hoping to get more game time as he gets back into full fitness.

Arsenal were linked with a move for Kroupi in the summer. His return to action has reignited interest in the player. A number of other European clubs also understood to be watching his situation.

Kroupi has attracted interest from a variety of top clubs including Manchester United, Tottenham, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain.

The French Under-21 international has impressed with his goal scoring in his first campaign in England. At only 20 years old, he has plenty of development to do under an experienced manager like Arteta.

However, Bournemouth are said to be reluctant to let Kroupi leave in January. Selling a bright young forward would leave Marco Rose with a tough decision to make.

It could get even more complicated if Alex Scott is also being seriously pursued. Chelsea and Liverpool are both linked with the midfielder.

Arsenal may therefore struggle to convince the Cherries to part with Kroupi during the winter window.

Another exciting option for Arsenal comes in the form of Juventus winger Yildiz. The winger has been linked with a move to North London for a number of transfer windows. He has once again been in the news recently at the end of the summer.

However, the Turkish international has struggled to get going on this campaign. He has only featured once in Serie A and has failed to feature since he suffered an injury.

Juventus have previously shown little interest in letting him leave. Head coach Luciano Spalletti firmly dismissed the prospect during the summer. Indicating that even an offer worth €100 million would not change the club’s position.

However, things could change next season. There are reports from Italy that Juventus may have to sell their star player if they fail to make the Champions League.

The Turin-based outfit are currently sitting in seventh spot in Serie A after just 10 games and are six points away from the qualifying spots.

This means that if they don’t make it into Europe, then it could put more pressure on Arsenal’s pursuit of Yildiz. It could create more pressure on them to raise funds.

Arsenal had a very busy summer with the addition of Bruno Guimaraes, Christos Tzolis, Ezri Konsa, Piero Hincapie and Illan Meslier.

But they also missed out on a few big names, such as Vinicius Jr and Julian Alvarez.

Despite this, there is still interest in Kroupi and Yildiz, suggesting that Arteta is still looking to strengthen his attacking options. Both players would bring quality and potential to the squad; however, there are some issues with both.

There are many unknowns surrounding this situation. Bournemouth aren’t keen to sell Kroupi and Juventus aren’t in a great financial position.

This doesn’t mean that either player will definitely be moving to the Emirates but much will depend on what happens at their clubs in the coming months.

Binance Says $6.34 Billion Hack Began With Fake Job Interview

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Binance’s incident report says the $6.34 billion Oct. 29 theft was a five-month campaign that began with a fake job interview and a poisoned developer tool.

The $6.34 billion theft from Binance began with a fake job interview and ran for five months before a single coin moved, the exchange said Tuesday in its first public account of the Oct. 29 attack.

Another initial incident report from Binance, released alongside a media briefing by co-CEO Richard Teng and chief security officer Jimmy Su, describes a campaign that combined a poisoned software download, a staged recruitment process, malware that evaded endpoint detection and an internal AI tool the attackers turned against the company’s own wallet engineers.

Binance said it has frozen or intercepted about $2.85 billion of the stolen assets and replenished 98% of affected tokens from its own funds, with the balance being bought on the open market.

“This wasn’t one mistake or one breach — it was a months-long campaign,” Teng wrote on X. “We’re publishing the full report because the lessons go far beyond Binance.”

The FBI has attributed the attack to North Korea. Binance’s report cites that finding but stops short of its own attribution. Pyongyang rejected the claim Monday, with Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, calling it a “grave political provocation” through state media.

According to Binance, the first foothold for this hack came in June. A wallet DevOps engineer searched for a popular AI coding tool and downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer.

Binance’s security team caught the anomaly, replaced the device and rotated credentials, but the episode exposed the engineer’s role and the names of colleagues on the wallet infrastructure team.

In September, a second engineer was approached on a legitimate job platform by someone posing as a project director. A video interview with a purported HR representative followed, with the interviewer sharing a personal social media account to build trust. A second interview with a supposed CEO ended with an “assignment”: a code repository the engineer was told to install on his work machine.

The repository replaced a legitimate pyenv component with a malicious version and opened a channel to an attacker-controlled server. Binance said the zero-day malware was not flagged by its endpoint tools at the time.

On Oct. 20, the attackers used that machine and an internal AI tool to reach two more wallet engineers, one of whom held a container deployment token. On Oct. 29, between 17:15 and 19:56 UTC, they logged into a third engineer’s computer, deployed a container with the stolen credentials and launched the drain. Binance said it blocked 57 other suspected North Korea-linked attempts this year using similar lures.

The money left fast. Between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, five hot wallets sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker address. Wallets on Solana and Optimism followed with about 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP. A Binance hot wallet then sent 18,270 BTC.

The attacker used the compromised signing service to invoke Ethereum’s EIP-7702, which lets an account delegate execution rights to a smart contract without exposing its key, and gave an attacker-controlled contract partial control of a Binance hot wallet.

Suspending withdrawals did not stop that last channel. The attackers had submitted 50 signing transactions to establish on-chain delegations that operated outside Binance’s withdrawal infrastructure. Because the wallet used multi-party computation, no single key existed to revoke them, and the team had to build a procedure on the spot. The final unauthorized transfer, 2,961.9 ETH, settled at 23:56 UTC.

Binance cleared the delegation at 00:10 UTC on Oct. 30.

The report acknowledges the gap. “These challenges extended the time required to fully contain the unauthorized asset movements,” it says, adding that the company is reviewing its signing policy coverage and hot wallet controls.

Customers withdrew $10.97 billion in the 46 hours after withdrawals reopened Sunday, with net outflows of $5.28 billion, according todata Teng shared Tuesday. By 03:00 UTC hourly deposits exceeded withdrawals, a shift Teng called a sign of stabilization. Binance reopened withdrawals for dozens more assets across nine networks on Tuesday.

The breach has become a talking point in Washington. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said the hack “proves our exact point” about the need for a federal registration path for offshore exchanges, and on Tuesday the agency cleared equity perpetual futures for U.S.-regulated venues, extending the onshoring push it began with Kalshi’s bitcoin perp in May.

Binance said it has rebuilt the wallet system and the internal AI tool in new environments, replaced affected devices, revoked the engineers’ credentials and expanded behavioral anomaly detection.

It is commissioning an independent review, raising spending on endpoint and developer-environment security and planning a research fund on AI security with outside firms. Some technical details, the report says, will stay private.

Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints.

The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One, found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis, which is known to increase the risk of heart failure.

This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation.

But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats (80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth.

"The message that we try to convey … is that the follow-up time is really important," study co-author John Baker, a professor of surgery in the Radiation Bioscience Laboratory at the Medical College of Wisconsin, told Live Science. "When astronauts come back to the Earth, they expect ‪—‬ and we expect ‪—‬ that they're going to live for a long time. I think we have to be wary that they could well develop at least some type of cardiac disease."

The link between exposure to radiation and cardiac issues has been well documented. However, "no astronaut has ever been exposed to galactic cosmic radiation for long periods of time," Baker said, which makes it difficult to determine exactly how space radiation affects the heart.

Although Baker and his team previously pinpointed cardiac issues among rats exposed to radiation, this new study utilized NASA's Simulated Galactic Cosmic Ray Simulation (SimGCRSim). This new simulator provides a more precise comparison of the levels of space radiation an astronaut might experience while exploring deep space for more than a year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

During the study, the researchers exposed rats to several minutes of radiation proportionate to their size, similar to what they might experience on a trip to Mars and back (a roughly 18-month round trip, with current technology). Some of the rats' hind legs were suspended, to "simulate conditions of weightlessness," Baker said.

After 360 days, the rats that were exposed to cosmic radiation developed twice as much scar tissue around the heart's small blood vessels than unexposed rats. This buildup of scar tissue means "the heart can't relax to the point when it needs to," thereby increasing the risk of heart failure, Baker said.

This effect was not seen in the rats who were exposed only to simulated weightlessness, confirming "it was only the radiation that produced the damaging effect on the heart," Baker said. However, long-term testing revealed that this group of rats had lower levels of key immune cells, suggesting that microgravity also may affect aspects of long-term health. (Numerous studies have shown various short-term health impacts related to microgravity.)

This study "is a very valuable contribution to space biology," Rupak Pathak, an associate professor of pharmaceutical science at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences who was not involved in the study but holds a doctorate in radiation biology, told Live Science. While rats and humans have clear differences, "they share more than 90% of genetic information," he said, as well as very similar cardiac systems.

Given that the study authors were able to expose the rats to radiation only once, Pathak would like to see further experiments exploring whether chronic radiation exposure affects the function of the heart and other vital organs.

Baker and his colleagues hope that future experiments can be used to help NASA implement safeguards for astronauts on long-term missions, such as providing astronauts heart medications or improving shielding for the spacecraft.

"The more we know before we start, then the better NASA is going to be at working out what types of countermeasures can be developed," said Baker.

Lenarczyk, M., Kronenberg, A., Kwok, A., Borg, A., Alsheikh, A. J., Mathison, A. J., Zimmermann, M. T., Lawton, S. B. R., Raff, H., Willey, J., Komorowski, R. A., Urrutia, R., & Baker, J. E. (2026). Multiple simulated spaceflight stressors impact cardiac fibrosis, calcium dynamics, immune function, cytokines and gene variants in rat, Rattus norvegicus. PLoS ONE, 21(9), e0357485. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0357485

Frontier Airlines Warns Of Scam Emails With Real Booking Codes And Fake Refunds

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

A fraudulent airline email is easier to dismiss when it gets your trip details wrong. What happens when it includes your actual flight information and confirmation number? Frontier Airlines passengers are reporting precisely that, with scammers using real reservation details to solicit credit card information. Frontier has confirmed an active phishing campaign, and the obvious question is how the scammers obtained the data.

View From The Wing highlights a concerning report that Frontier customers have received fraudulent emails offering refunds or claiming an existing reservation has a payment problem.

The troubling part is that passengers say the messages contain genuine confirmation numbers and flight details. Some report entering their credit card information into the linked websites.

One version promises a refund after the passenger verifies the card used for the booking. Another creates urgency by suggesting payment for an upcoming trip has not gone through.

The latter is a scammer’s dream: someone expecting to travel soon may be particularly inclined to resolve what appears to be a ticketing problem.

Frontier has published a warning on its website, acknowledging an active email phishing campaign targeting customers.

The airline says it will not email passengers asking them to revalidate a reservation, reconfirm credit card information, or provide payment details to obtain a refund.

The critical point is that a correct confirmation number does not make an email legitimate.

If the passenger reports are accurate, someone has obtained information that should not be available to a random scammer. That raises the possibility of unauthorized access to a reservation-related system, compromised credentials, or misuse by someone with legitimate access.

An inside job is one possibility. A breach at the airline or a service provider is another. Compromised passenger email accounts could also expose booking confirmations, though it seems too coincidental if this has been happening on a larger scale and only with Frontier.

We do not yet have enough evidence to identify the source, establish how broadly information was exposed, or conclude that the access happened recently. Older stolen data can still be used in a new scam campaign.

There is, however, a relevant disclosure. In an October 2, 2026 notification, Frontier described a security incident involving its customer care database and information submitted through its customer care form. The airline said it updated the database configuration and improved monitoring in response.

That disclosure does not establish that this phishing campaign is linked to that incident, but it makes the question of where these reservation details originated even harder to ignore.

Warning passengers is necessary…but it would be nice if Frontier was a bit more transparent about the source of the leak.

I recently questioned Lufthansa Group’s decision to require a Travel ID account for online check-in. My objection was to making passengers create an account to complete a basic task after buying a ticket.

This Frontier story gives me reason to consider the security side more closely.

A booking reference and surname are convenient credentials, but they can be copied from a confirmation email or exposed elsewhere. Requiring additional authentication before allowing access to sensitive reservation information could offer passengers protection, even if it still strikes me as a bit heavy-handed like the incessant two-factor-authorization to log into Air Canada Aeroplan or United MileagePlus.

I’m not convinced Lufthansa introduced its requirement for this reason, or that its particular implementation would prevent the Frontier scam. Still, I would be more receptive to an account requirement accompanied by a clear explanation of what it protects and why the existing process is inadequate. Communication goes a long way in just about everything…

Frontier has confirmed a phishing campaign, while passengers report that fraudulent messages include their real booking details. For now, verify any supposed payment problem or refund through the airline’s official website or app. Do not trust a message merely because it contains your personal details.

But the burden should not fall entirely on passengers to spot convincing fraud. Frontier needs to explain, to the extent its investigation can establish, how scammers obtained the information that makes these messages so believable.

An Indian passenger died and two more were injured when two helicopters crashed while landing near Everest Base Camp this morning.

The helicopters were operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two of Nepal’s largest companies. The crash occurred at the helipad on the outskirts of the village of Pheriche (4,371m). It’s a typical spot for helicopters to stop and refuel when on their way to and from Everest Base Camp.

As shown in the horrific video below, the two helicopters came from different directions, and both tried to land at the same time. Somehow their rotor blades collided. The inexplicable crash occurred in a wide, flat area with good visibility.

Vasanth Kumar, an Indian trekker, died on the spot, The Tourism Times reported. Shailesh Kishan from New Zealand and Rabindra Prajapati, a senior captain, were seriously injured. Both have been airlifted to hospitals in Kathmandu. They were all on board the Fishtail Air helicopter. The Air Dynasty chopper was carrying cargo.

Former workshop converted into contemporary Japanese home with "a sense of the passage of time"

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Japanese studio Akio Isshiki Architects has transformed the home and workshop of a sheet-metal craftsperson in the castle town of Tatsuno into a modern house with a latticed wooden gate.

Architect Akio Isshiki, the founder of the eponymous studio, said he had to take a lot of different aspects into consideration when designing the project.

Among them was the location, as the two-storey home is located in a historic town known for being built around a medieval mountain castle.

“The project explores an architecture that responds naturally to the many contexts and conditions surrounding the house: the historic streetscape of the former castle town, traces of the former owner’s work as a sheet-metal craftsman, the client’s wishes, and practical constraints such as building regulations and structural requirements,” Isshiki told Dezeen.

For example, while the client had initially wanted a deck that would be connected to the dining room, the compact site made such a design difficult.

Instead, Isshiki removed part of the existing interior of the dining room to create a terrace space, which also includes a traditional-style engawa platform to connect the home with the garden.

Here, the studio added a sliding glass door that was designed so that its frame is hidden in the wall when it is closed, creating the impression of a fully open space.

Isshiki also wanted the 144-square-metre contemporary home to nod to more traditional Japanese houses.

“To sit comfortably within the townscape that retains the character of a former castle town, the spatial principles of traditional machiya – Japanese old townhouses – have been incorporated into this contemporary residence,” he explained.

“Examples include a long approach leading towards a bright garden at the back of the house, and an engawa, a narrow platform that connects the interior with the garden.”

The former workshop in front of the house was treated as a public-facing space. Where it looks onto the street, Isshiki added a large latticed, sliding gate, made from cedar, as well as a narrow entrance porch.

Inside, this multi-functional space becomes almost like an enclosed terrace. Here, Isshiki also added a small wooden toilet, inspired by those found in traditional machiya houses.

The studio kept a number of objects that were found in the old workshop, including a metal ring that now decorates a handrail next to the indoor staircase.

Isshiki relocated this staircase so that it sits at the front of the house, in the old workshop space – one of the biggest changes made to the layout of the house. A stone underneath the first step provides a space to remove footwear.

Isshiki’s studio used wood throughout the renovation, as the original building was made from timber and this material worked best with the existing neighbourhood, including a historic shrine that stands directly across from the house.

“The newly added wood, including the doors, is cedar, which is also the primary wood used in the original structure,” Isshiki said.

“Cedar is one of the most widely used types of wood in Japan and is readily available,” he continued.

“The contrast between the lighter new cedar and the existing cedar, which has darkened with age, brings a sense of the passage of time to the house.”

Akio Isshiki Architects also used earthen plasterwork in the home to create a tactile feel, while Tunisian tiles add decorative patterns in the kitchen. Here, the studio also created a built-in, combined wooden dining table and work surface.

On the top floor, which has a bedroom, living room and guest room, the studio mostly kept the original layout.

However, it added a sunken study space and a tokonoma, a recessed area used to display flowers and pieces of art.

“Through careful consideration of spatial dimensions, light, connections to the outdoors, materials, details, and relationships between spaces, the aim was to create a home that feels comfortable as a whole,” Isshiki concluded about the renovation.

His studio has previously designed a charred-cedar-clad house in Osaka and married old and new within a combined home and restaurant.

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said it had deployed its epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million of additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department said it has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

Target Soho Redesign Brings NYC Streetscapes Indoors

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

The Target red bullseye offers near-instant brand recognition. No matter which location they enter, shoppers know what to expect from the big-box retailer. That’s not quite the case at New York’s Soho location. Less than a year after reimagining its first floor, Target has unveiled a redesigned lower level by Something Special Studios that encourages exploration and discovery.

Located at the corner of Broadway and Houston Street, Target Soho was initially conceived as a “living lab” where the brand could test new ideas for the future of retail, according to Gigi Guerra, Target’s VP of Marketing, Creative Curation. Since opening 10 months ago, the location has offered a more curated, design-led shopping experience. The new lower level extends that approach to everyday categories, including home, wellness, toys, and food and beverage.

“We’re rethinking each of these categories as destinations,” Guerra says, “making everyday shopping more intuitive, engaging, and full of unexpected discoveries.”

To bring this idea to life, Target turned to New York- and LA-based Something Special Studios. “We started with the idea of making the everyday feel worth discovering,” studio founder Michael Goldberg says. “Soho is a neighborhood defined by its historic character and constant reinvention, and we wanted the Lower Level to reflect that energy while staying true to Target’s playful, optimistic point of view.”

Familiar New York spaces, such as the ubiquitous local bodega or compact apartment, became starting points for the design. Rather than recreating them literally, the studio reinterpreted these environments as distinct shopping destinations. For instance, Bullseye Loft uses domestic vignettes to showcase home products, while The Snack Bar recalls a New York streetscape with corner stores and newsstands.

The design also had to respond to the constraints of the existing cast-iron commercial building. Its column grid, lightwell, escalators, and other architectural elements influenced the layout, with the existing row of columns becoming the central avenue that organizes the floor.

For all its distinct destinations, the layout still needed to be easy to navigate and shop. “We approached the floor as a journey that guests can experience at their own pace,” Goldberg says. “The central avenue provides a clear organizing spine, with wider pathways and intuitive sightlines connecting a series of curated destinations.”

Although the zones have distinct identities, there aren’t hard boundaries between them. “Lighting, material shifts, and architectural thresholds” help distinguish the areas, Goldberg explains. He adds: “Ultimately, every decision needed to balance function with delight, giving people a reason to slow down and explore while ensuring the store remains easy to navigate.”

Something Special Studios incorporated brushed and orbital-finished aluminum, tinted mirrors, glossy lacquer, fabric awnings, and integrated lighting to give the retail space a more polished, contemporary character. Wood, meanwhile, introduces warmth and contrast. “The mix is durable and functional, but still tactile and expressive,” Goldberg says.

Target Red, a brand standard, remains part of the Soho store’s identity, but it’s joined by Cherry Stain Red, a custom color developed for the store. Goldberg explains that it’s part of a broader palette of warm neutrals. “Together, these tones establish a cohesive visual identity while allowing the Lower Level to develop its own character,” he says. “The palette creates continuity with the floor above, while warmer materials, reflective surfaces, and tactile finishes give the Lower Level a more metropolitan feel.”

Beyond Soho, Cherry Stain Red will be introduced across the chain for Target’s new Beauty Studio concept, an example of how the location serves as a testing ground for the retailer. “[The Soho location] serves as a test-and-learn platform where we can experiment, learn, and evolve,” Guerra says. “We’re creating more intentional environments that give everyday categories a stronger point of view.”

This approach allows destinations like Balance Mart, for wellness products, and Explorers’ Lab, for toys and entertainment, to showcase trending brands, new collaborations, and seasonal products. Yet, despite the more immersive environment, the store still needs to function like a Target. As Goldberg explains, shoppers should be able to come in, find what they need quickly, and leave—or take their time exploring.

“The completed Target Soho store reflects our belief that great design is about more than how a space looks—it’s about how people experience it,” Guerra says. “Every element is designed to make everyday shopping feel a little more unexpected and inspiring.”

Researchers identified a 5,300-year-old kidney stone in the burial of a Bronze Age cattle herder in Russia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Bronze Age man buried in a monumental tomb near the Black Sea may have died from complications of a urinary tract infection (UTI) more than five millennia ago, according to a new study. Archaeologists identified a grape-size object consistent with a kidney or bladder stone in the man's burial.

"He lived with a chronic urogenital infection," study lead author Natalia Berezina, an anthropologist at Lomonosov Moscow State University in Russia, told Live Science in an email.

"It was not a brief episode," she said. "His last years were probably marked by considerable and more or less constant pain."

Berezina and colleagues investigated a small, stone-like object found in an Early Bronze Age burial in the Stavropol Upland region of southwestern Russia. They published their findings Sept. 30 in the journal Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences.

The burial was part of a kurgan cemetery, an ancient steppe funeral tradition that involved constructing a large mound of dirt over a grave. Archaeologists discovered a catacomb when they excavated the mound, and inside was the skeleton of a man who was in his 40s when he died around 5,300 years ago. The researchers found a flint arrowhead near the man's pelvis.

But during a laboratory analysis after the skeleton was excavated, researchers noticed an odd stone-like object in the collection of hand bones. The brownish object was round with several protrusions and measured about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) in diameter, or roughly the size of a grape. A small crack in the object showed a crystal-like structure inside.

To learn more, the researchers used several analytical methods to determine what the tiny object was made of. First, X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed that the main components of the object were calcium and phosphorus. Then, they used X-ray powder diffraction analysis to identify the crystal structures.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In addition to common minerals, the researchers discovered the presence of whitlockite, a rare calcium salt that is known to occur in kidney, bladder and prostate stones. These "stones," collectively called calculi, are hard masses of minerals, such as calcium-containing salts. They differ in terms of the organ they form within, the exact mechanism of how they form, and their chemical makeup, although kidney and bladder stones tend to contain very similar compounds.

Whitlockite is strongly associated with bacterial infections in the human body, which suggests that the Bronze Age man had a chronic infection that resulted in the stone, the scientists concluded.

"On the balance of the available evidence, we regard a renal [kidney] stone secondary to chronic upper urinary tract infection as the most probable origin," the researchers wrote. That is, the man dealt with chronic or recurrent UTIs, which led to the formation of the stone and likely caused him considerable discomfort. UTIs can contribute to the formation of kidney stones by altering the acidity of urine and making minerals more likely to accumulate.

The researchers aren't sure why the man had urinary tract issues or whether it contributed to his death.

Notably, kidney stones can sometimes travel to the bladder, so it's unclear exactly where the stone was in the man's body when he died. If the stone had obstructed the man's ureter ‪—‬ one of the two long tubes that connect the kidneys to the bladder ‪—‬ it may have caused kidney swelling, a secondary infection or sepsis. These conditions were frequently fatal prior to the invention of antibiotics.

Other possibilities for what caused the stone include a bacterial infection of the man's prostate gland or even a sexually transmitted infection.

The man was likely on the move frequently within this Early Bronze Age steppe society, and other injuries to his skeleton suggested he had a physically demanding life, the researchers wrote. His bones showed that he was well muscled but was also dealing with degenerative joint disease in his spine, shoulders, hips, hands and feet. He had a series of healed fractures in his right shoulder, ribs and forearm.

"These were people who worked with cattle and heavy wagons on the open steppe," Berezina said, "and the injuries that follow from that are the injuries we find." In a previous study at a nearby cemetery, Berezina and colleagues found the skeleton of a man who was injured when a wagon ran over him, several years before his death. "Against that background, four healed fractures in our man look unremarkable," she said.

But the urinary tract stone would have made the man's life difficult, the researchers noted. "This individual suffered from a painful and debilitating chronic urogenital infection, a condition that would have significantly impacted his quality of life," they wrote.

Berezina, N. Ya., Statkus, M. A., Kalmykov, A. A., Abdrashitova, I. V., Kolesnik, I. V., Platonov, V. B., Shashurin, D. A., Garmay, A. V., Korobkova, V. V., Ryleeva, V. S., & Gresky, J. (2026). Urolithiasis in the Early Bronze Age of the North Caucasus: A paleopathological case study and insights into ancient lifeways. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, 18(10), 209. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-026-02574-7

Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

Hinge Health revenue jumps 52% in Q3 as it expands beyond MSK, eyes hardware acquisitions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hinge Health is seeing early traction with its migraine and gastrointestinal care programs as it pushes beyond musculoskeletal care and builds a broader, multi-condition platform.

But the company's core MSK business remains the engine fueling its robust growth.

"Our vision has always been to automate the delivery of care using technology to close the gap between the care people need and the care they actually receive. We're now applying that same approach and the same trusted relationships with employers and partners in neurology and gastrointestinal care," Daniel Perez, Hinge Health co-founder and CEO, told analysts and investors on the third-quarter earnings call Monday. "We're not starting from scratch in each new category. We're extending a platform that's already proven into conditions that are often connected to the ones we already treat. We believe that's a fundamentally different and more powerful way to expand than what other companies in our space are attempting."

During a Q&A with analysts and investors on the earnings call, Perez asserted, "We’re not taking our eye off the ball in MSK. I think we’re actually widening our lead on MSK … But it’s allowing us to expand into other areas as well."

In the third quarter, the company posted $235 million in revenue, up 52% from $154 million a year ago, and above its guidance range of $223 million to $225 million. The company posted third-quarter adjusted earnings of 66 cents per share, exceeding Wall Street analysts' estimates of 60 cents per share. Hinge Health's non-GAAP income from operations increased 154% to $77.2 million in the third quarter.

Hinge Health, which launched in late 2014 and went public in May 2025, developed software combined with AI to automate physical therapy services for joint and muscle health. The company has designed its platform to address a broad spectrum of MSK care, including acute injury, chronic pain and post-surgical rehabilitation. To address the automation of care, Hinge has developed AI-powered motion tracking technology, a proprietary FDA-cleared wearable device called Enso, and an AI-supported care team to deliver scalable and personalized MSK care.

The company reported strong client growth, with 3,270 clients as of September 30, up 28% from a year ago. Last twelve months (LTM) calculated billings increased 54% year-over-year to $960 million as of September 30, compared to $624 million during Q3 2025.

The company also benefited from strong operational efficiency as it reported a gross margin of 87% in Q3, compared to 82% during the same quarter a year ago.

Free cash flow for the quarter was $113 million, representing a 51% free cash flow margin. The company ended the September quarter with total cash and equivalents of $359 million.

Based on strong Q3 and year-to-date results, Hinge Health boosted its 2026 outlook, now expecting full-year revenue to reach between $879 million and $881 million, reflecting year-over-year growth of 50% at the midpoint. That compares to the prior revenue target of $856 million to $860 million. The company now projects non-GAAP income from operations to be between $266 million and $268 million, reflecting year-over-year growth of 123% and non-GAAP operating margin of 30% at the midpoint.

Core MSK is still the company's largest revenue contributor by a wide margin, Perez noted, and that business is growing robustly. "We expect it to remain that way for years to come; the opportunity at MSK remains massively underpenetrated," Perez said.

"The MSK opportunity is still enormous. Musculoskeletal conditions are among the leading drivers of disability and healthcare spend in the United States, and the vast majority of people in America still don't have access to a digital MSK solution," Perez said during the call.

"We built something that works clinically, commercially, and economically, and we're still in the early innings of penetrating that market. We are the undisputed leader in this space, and we estimate 88% of lives within our markets are yet to be won, leaving a long runway for growth. That alone is a multi-year growth opportunity," he said.

The company is building on top of that MSK care foundation as it expands into migraine care and gastrointestinal care. Hinge acquired GI startup Cylinder Health in August for $105 million in cash.

The company's client base is up almost 30% year-over-year for its MSK care program and roughly 40% for its new GI Care Program since the acquisition announcement of Cylinder Health in August, Perez noted.

The company expects to make more acquisitions and is even looking at hardware acquisitions, Perez said. "I think too many technology companies, especially in healthcare, focus exclusively on software, but I absolutely firmly believe you will not automate care delivery without also investing in hardware. And we've shown we're pretty good at hardware," he said as the company internally developed its Enso wearable device.

Perez told Bloomberg last month that the company was interested in hardware that can augment virtual care.

"We will build organically first and use M&A when it accelerates our timeline. And our acquisitions, particularly in hardware, have historically been small tuck-ins of technology in a team, and then you build it out into something much larger," he added.

Looking at the company's new care programs, Perez called out notable early results from Hinge's migraine program, which is still in early access: 23% reduction in monthly migraine days, 28% reduction in migraine duration, equivalent to roughly five hours and just over half of surveyed members achieved a clinically meaningful improvement.

"We're also seeing a meaningful reduction in monthly prescription use days, which matters both for members and for the clients paying for their care," Perez said.

More than 800 clients, representing 9 million lives, now have access to the migraine program, approximately double the previous quarter, according to management. The migraine program was announced in May.

For the GI care business, Hinge Health is taking Cylinder's existing program and building it into the same app and care infrastructure it uses for MSK and migraine. The company is targeting summer 2027 for the fully integrated product. Meaningful revenue contribution should emerge particularly in 2028, after Hinge gets a fuller sales cycle with the integrated product, Perez noted.

Hinge Health sees an opportunity to offer health plans and employers one integrated care platform that covers multiple health conditions rather than separate point solutions.

Nearly one in two people with GI conditions also have MSK pain, and 70% of people withmigraine also have a GI condition, Perez noted.

"GI cost has been a growing pain point for employers and health plans, especially with the growth of GLP-1s, given GI side effects are so common, and our employer clients are very grateful for taking this on," he said during the call.

Hinge Health had a strong selling season in Q3, according to Aaryn Pure, Hinge Health's chief commercial officer, with three new Fortune 15 clients. "We've already received verbal agreements on more lives this year than we closed in all of last year, and last year was a record-breaking sales year for adding eligible lives," Pure noted.

More than 10 million lives across over 800 clients have access to multiple Hinge products, he said.

Small and midsize businesses are becoming an important growth channel for the company, even though Hinge began investing in that market just a year ago. Through Q3, Hinge Health closed nearly 1 million SMB lives, "demonstrating we're not just winning at the top of the market, we're adding clients across every size tier," Pure said on the call.

He also noted that some health plan and third-party administrator (TPA) partners are implementing or considering arrangements where Hinge Health is automatically embedded or offered on an opt-out basis in their SMB book of business.

"Being the first-mover preferred partner is allowing us to capture that market," Pure said.

The company also announced Monday that Jim Pursley will step down as president, effective January 1, and will join Hinge Health's board of directors. Following this transition, Pure will lead the commercial organization, the company said.

In an analyst note, Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote that Hinge Health demonstrates "market leadership with significant advantages both on the product and go-to-market fronts."

"With a nearly 150% increase in shares YTD, HNGE now trades at approximately 11 times our 2027 adjusted gross profit, a premium to mature, high-margin, growth-oriented healthcare IT peers. Still, at these levels, we believe the stock presents a compelling long-term risk/reward and see continued growth momentum and upside to operating income and free cash flow estimates," Daniels wrote.

Yinka Ilori reveals Tottenham Hotspur away shirt

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has collaborated with Premier League football team Tottenham Hotspur to create a customised version of the club’s colourful away shirt.

Ilori reimagined the colourful away shirt, which has a pattern with “never-before-seen visuals inspired by never-before-seen destinations”, by adding a graphic to the front and back.

On the front, in the position the sponsor logo is usually located, Ilori designed a circular motif combining the football club’s initials – THFC – with an abbreviation for London and the postcode for Tottenham, LDN17.

The lettering is bright orange with a white background.

On the rear of the shirt, Ilori created a graphic in his typical playful style around the letters COYS, which stands for Come On You Spurs.

Encircling the letters are the words “I know I am, I’m sure I am”, with the words “We are Tottenham wherever we go” around the whole graphic.

All of the lettering uses Ilori’s custom typeface, which was designed by type foundry British Standard Type for the designer in 2024.

According to the designer, who grew up in north London where the Populous-designed Tottenham Hotspur stadium is located, the collaboration aims to demonstrate the power of football to unite people.

“This project is a celebration of belonging and the power of football to bring people together,” said Ilori.

“For me, football is about the wider culture and the incredible sense of unity that comes from standing on the terraces, chanting alongside thousands of others,” he continued.

“I wanted the design to honour Tottenham Hotspur’s heritage while capturing that collective joy and spirit. The ‘Never Far From Home’ message really resonated with me, reflecting how football has the power to make you feel at home, wherever you are.”

The shirt is the latest design from the designer who has recently collaborated with brands including Brabantia and Veuve Clicquot.

Ilori also recently created a homeware and furniture collection for department store Dunelm.

More than 60% of respondents in a 2026 Goldman Sachs survey of 5,106 working and retired Americans said they had taken work outside their primary job, most out of necessity rather than a wish for extra spending money. Nearly 70% had delayed a major financial goal.

Retirement is increasingly becoming a touchy topic for many, especially those of us who are used to a certain level of stability.

The news only makes matters worse. On Friday, October 30, we saw Nasdaq’s biggest 1-day drop since June 5, setting the internet ablaze with speculation. The index closed 7.8% below its October 6 record, though it was noted that the S&P 500 was only a few percent below its own record.

Then there’s inflation. Annual inflation reached 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August. Pair that with continuing international conflicts on several fronts, and you’ve got the perfect storm of insecurity.

A National Institute on Retirement Security survey found that 80% of Americans say that the nation faces a retirement crisis and 61% worry they won’t be financially secure in retirement.

The respondents blamed inflation (73%) and market volatility (62%) as contributing factors, and 76% feared Social Security cuts if Congress fails to act.

A New York Life survey of more than 2,000 adults found that 34% had already delayed retirement or planned to, and 46% of them expected to push it back 5 years or more. Their top reasons were a lack of savings (46%) and inflation (45%).

Those who have already retired aren’t immune to these insecurities. The Goldman Sachs sample included 1,494 retirees aged 45 to 75. A market drop may also hurt more when you’re drawing from a portfolio than when you’re adding to it.

So, wondering if you should go back to work feels like a warranted question. Plenty of retirees take the leap back. Doctors go back too, though plenty of them say they don’t miss it. In a recent r/emergencymedicine thread, retired ED physicians were split on the question.

One, 3 years out, said he doesn’t miss it at all and still has the occasional nightmare. Another quit at 61 with no plan, misses the people and belonging to the group and keeps looking for work without luck.

1.5 million retirees reentered the workforce by March 2022.

We spend decades planning for the day we stop working. Then some of us stop, and a year or 2 later we’re checking job boards or answering calls from our old group. If that sounds like you, this article is for you.

Let’s take a look at the reasons many doctors feel the urge to un-retire, what going back to work in 2026 entails and the logistics of it all.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

In case you missed it: Micro-retirements aren’t a shortcut to FIRE

Money is the top reason many retirees choose to go back, so let’s start there. A recent survey found that 48% of working retirees said they needed the income, while 45% said they worked for social and emotional benefits.

Divide 1 year of spending by your portfolio. An example in T. Rowe Price’s example illustrates a 62-year-old with $900,000 who spends $65,000 a year.

That’s a 7.2% withdrawal rate. She has a 64% chance of not outliving her money if she retires at 62, a 91% chance at 65 and a 97% chance at 67.

Now let’s imagine a physician-specific version.

Say you have $2,500,000 and spend $150,000 a year before taxes. That’s a 6% withdrawal rate. A part-time job paying $60,000 would trim your withdrawals to $90,000, which is 3.6%.

You lower your rate by 2.4 percentage points without changing how you live. Of course, taxes will reduce that paycheck so ask your planner for a clearer outline.

One retired doctor said he saved about 30% of his take-home pay in his last years of full-time work, and his spending ended up around half of his colleagues’.

He could walk away any day, and his group knew it. That kind of freedom is helpful even after you return because you’re able to negotiate better when you don’t actually need the job.

Before you take a job, figure out whether the problem is your portfolio or your spending. If your withdrawal rate looks fine but spending still makes you uneasy, a concrete spending plan may help more than a paycheck. Ask your planner to set a monthly amount you can spend without second-guessing.

Working longer also helps in 2 other ways. You can delay account withdrawals as well as Social Security. Benefits grow 8% for every year you wait past full retirement age until you reach 70, while claiming at 62 cuts them by almost 30%.

Continuing to work also gives you more time to contribute to your retirement accounts. If your new employer offers a 401(k) or 403(b), the 2026 limit is $24,500, plus an $8,000 catch-up at 50 and older or $11,250 at ages 60 to 63.

It depends on whether you’ve claimed it and how old you are. If you haven’t claimed, going back to work is straightforward and your eventual monthly SS check will continue to increase.

If you claimed before full retirement age (FRA), the earnings test applies. In 2026, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 if you’re under FRA all year.

In the year you reach FRA, the limit rises to $65,160, and the agency withholds $1 for every $3 above it. Only earnings before the month you reach FRA count.

If your part-time schedule pays more than $24,480, expect withholding. The money isn’t gone for good, though. Social Security recalculates your benefit at FRA to credit the months it withheld.

Only wages and self-employment earnings count, so investment income doesn’t trigger withholding. Once you reach FRA, working doesn’t reduce your benefit.

You’ll also keep paying Social Security taxes on your paychecks. Higher earnings can also make more of your benefit taxable, so ask your tax preparer to estimate that too.

What if you changed your mind after claiming early? If you claimed before FRA, you have 12 months to withdraw your application. You must repay what you received, and Social Security then treats your record as if you never claimed at all.

Coverage before 65 costs far more in 2026 than it did in 2025 since the enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025.

KFF reports that a 60-year-old with a $65,000 income now pays an average of $10,389 more per year, or $865 per month. The subsidy cliff is also back which means above 400% of the poverty level (which is $62,600 for a single person in 2026), you lose the premium tax credit entirely.

On top of that, the ACA allows insurers to charge adults in their 60s up to 3 times what they charge adults in their 20s.

So a job with group health coverage may save you thousands of dollars a year because it skips the marketplace and the income cliff.

A working physician said that if he left medicine early, he’d take a flexible management job of about 25 hours a week mostly for the group insurance and the 401(k) match.

If you’re considering the same, ask HR what hours are required for benefits and when coverage starts, since each plan sets its own cutoff.

Medicare changes much of the picture. If you delayed Part B because you had coverage through your own or your spouse’s current job, you get an 8-month special enrollment period after that job or coverage ends.

If you miss it, you’ll have to pay 10% more for each full 12-month period you could have had Part B, for as long as you keep it. COBRA and retiree coverage don’t count for that exemption.

Keep in mind that Medicare generally pays first if the employer has fewer than 20 employees. So a small practice’s plan may pay second and you’d still need Part B.

Learn more: 11 Retirement Planning Mistakes That Haunt High-Earning Physicians

Don’t count on getting your old job back.

An AARP survey of more than 3,500 people ages 50 and older found that 74% believe their age will be a barrier to getting hired, and 64% of workers 50 and older have seen or experienced age discrimination at work. That stigma is even worse for women.

Another AARP report found that 37% of workers 50 and older experienced subtle age discrimination during a job search in 2025, up from 30% in 2024. These surveys cover all fields, not only medicine, so ask recruiters in your specialty what they are seeing firsthand.

Think about what you want the next job to be. 24% of workers 50 and older planned a job change in 2025, so you won’t be the only one looking. If your retirement was driven mostly due to clinical work, teaching, consulting or chart review may suit you better than your old schedule.

We’ve already established that money drives about half of all unretirements. Boredom and a wish to help others drive many of the rest.

In an AARP survey, 18% of unretirees said boredom or a desire to stay active was their main reason for returning to work. For doctors, these sentiments start even before they leave.

In a Jackson Physician Search survey, 44% of physicians feared losing their sense of purpose in retirement and 39% feared boredom (money was still the top fear at 53%).

In CHG Healthcare’s 2024 survey, physicians who wanted to keep working felt that way because of a love of medicine (58%), social connections (57%) and concern for patients (39%). Others stated not feeling emotionally ready (47%), wanting to keep their lifestyle (35%) and fearing boredom or isolation (33%).

In Medscape’s 2025 retirement report, the top reason physicians gave for not retiring earlier was feeling they still had more to offer (62%), ahead of not having enough saved (45%). In the 2023 report, 46% expected retirement to feel like losing a part of their identity.

Retired and soon-to-retire ED physicians on Reddit offer a mixed bag of insights. One commenter who was 4 months from retiring expects to miss the ego boost of being a doctor. The one who quit at 61 with no plan misses colleagues and most of his patients, though not the fatigue of rotating shifts or the dread of sending home someone who should have stayed. Several said sleep and a normal daytime rhythm were the biggest change.

Retirement also changes what stresses you out. A 2025 Mayo Clinic review of physician well-being in retirement says that stress moves from work problems to personal ones, including professional identity, family, health and the loss of relationships.

The journal’s late-career paper urges physicians to plan for social and emotional needs along with finances. If you can’t picture your days without the work and the people, look at part-time options before you retire fully.

Give your first year in retirement a fair shake before you decide. People who leave long, consuming careers often describe a rocky start to retirement.

One user on Reddit said that it took about a year to stop feeling guilty about doing nothing. Another lasted 2 years, took a part-time job and has stayed 10 years. A third said the new job mattered to them mostly for the community, since all their friends still worked.

In case you missed it: The Nightmare Before Retirement: A Physician’s Cautionary Tale (2026 Edition)

If burnout pushed you out in the first place, the same job will push you out again. In 2026, burnout in healthcare is still running rampant.

Doximity’s May 2026 poll found that 82% of physicians say they’re overworked and 46% are considering early retirement because of it.

That number is up from 37% in 2025 and 21% in 2021. The jump is sharpest among women (54% in 2026 compared to 33% in 2023) and physicians ages 50 to 54 (56%, up from 35%).

Medscape’s 2026 burnout report corroborates this. 50% of male and 51% of female physicians say that their work causes their burnout, and 13%–14% are considering leaving medicine altogether.

In a MedCentral survey, 44% of physicians said they had considered leaving medical practice since the start of the year.

A recent AMA study in The Permanente Journal looked at doctors who had already left and found that 971 clinically inactive physicians were typically 48.1 years old when they left clinical practice. Their top reasons were the hassle factor (44.7%), stress (44.5%), unrealistic patient demands (41.1%) and lack of professional satisfaction (38.4%).

Most doctors don’t plan to go cold turkey, however. In CHG Healthcare’s late-career survey, 63% of respondents said they’d rather work less than not work at all and 94% had at least slight interest in locum tenens work.

26% of physicians from a Weatherby Healthcare survey say that they are interested in locum tenens work. That’s 7 points higher than last year and the highest in 10 years.

If the actual reason behind your retirement still rings true or any of the reasons stated above give you a pause, you may want to reconsider jumping back into the workforce. Unless financial insecurity is twisting your arm, there’s no point in going back to something that already burned you out.

Fortunately, there are many other work options for physicians that don’t involve selling your soul. Locum tenens and expert witness work are popular ways for physicians to keep working.

Learn more: Physician Side Gigs That Actually Pay in 2026

Rules vary by state so check what’s needed where you live. Florida requires a reactivation fee, proof of continuing medical education (CME) for each year the license was inactive or retired, a health history and a financial responsibility form.

Pennsylvania requires full Board review and possibly proof of competency. According to the AAMC some states require a reentry program after an absence that averages about 3 years.

The ED physician who quit at 61 let his board certification lapse and said he now wishes he’d kept it, because it might have opened insurance work.

Another retired ED doctor commented that he dreamed for 2 years about working shifts without a license or malpractice cover. The roles you want to work in may or may not require these credentials so check before you make up your mind.

Most carriers give retiring physicians tail coverage free or at low cost. But some carriers may cancel that tail or charge a premium if you resume practice because when you return to clinical practice and receive pay or compensation for clinical work, you violate the retirement condition under which the tail fee was waived. Check with your provider.

The AMA warns that some physicians’ retirement income may change if they take paid work. Check your pension plan before you accept a role.

Of course, there’s no universal right answer and no rulebook that says you must make one permanent decision.

Start by being honest about why you feel the urge to return. If it’s your portfolio that’s got you worried, earning an income may give you some much-needed breathing room.

If you miss the people, intellectual challenge or sense of purpose, you might find what you’re looking for in a very different role.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

But if you’re simply uncomfortable with having more time than you’ve ever had before, give yourself a little longer before dusting off your resume.

Most importantly, don’t let a bad week in the market convince you that decades of retirement planning have failed. Nor should you feel obliged to return to medicine because you miss being a physician. It’s okay to miss parts of your career without wanting the whole thing back.

And no matter what you decide, don’t let your credentials lapse. Your medical license and board certification represent years of hard work and keeping them active preserves options you may not realize you’ll want later.

Even if you’re 100% certain you’ll never practice again, give your future self the benefit of the doubt. You don’t have to use those credentials, but you might one day wish you still had them.

Also read: The Idea of “Retiring to” Something

It depends on your finances, personal goals and reasons for retiring. Returning to work can provide income, health insurance and social connections, but it shouldn’t come at the expense of the retirement you worked so hard to achieve.

The most common reasons include financial insecurity, boredom, loss of purpose, social isolation and missing the intellectual challenge of their former careers.

Yes. Retired physicians can return to clinical practice, provided they meet their state medical board’s licensing and reactivation requirements. They may also need to address CME, board certification and malpractice coverage.

Yes, if you claim Social Security before full retirement age. In 2026, benefits are withheld if your earnings exceed $24,480, or $65,160 in the year you reach full retirement age. The earnings test no longer applies once you reach FRA.

Keeping your medical license active preserves the option to return to clinical practice without going through the full reactivation process. Check your state’s renewal requirements and consider maintaining board certification, too.

There’s no set waiting period. Give yourself time to adjust to retirement and understand what’s driving your desire to return. If finances aren’t forcing the decision, consider giving retirement at least a year before making a move.

TB 26-10 Printed Circuit Board Assembly Chip Resistor Body Cracking

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

For more information, contact Joel W. Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov.

Chip resistors are widely used in NASA projects, yet cases of alumina substrate cracking during environmental testing are rare. Two instances of thick-film chip resistor cracking were observed during thermal cycling after vibration, with fractures occurring across the short axis due to bending. Failure analyses ruled out defective lots and fatigue, identifying board flexure, component orientation, excessive solder, and mounting stresses as contributing factors. The bulletin recommends careful component placement, finite element analysis, controlled solder fillet height, thorough inspection, and functional thermal shock testing to mitigate flexure-induced cracking risks in ceramic body components on printed circuit boards.

BackgroundThe NESC noted historical lack of reported cases of chip resistors’ alumina substrate cracking during vibration and thermal cycling, although chip resistors are ubiquitous across NASA projects. Two instances of thick film chip resistor body cracking were observed during environmental acceptance testing on printed circuit board assemblies. Both failures occurred during thermal cycling after vibration testing, exhibiting intermittent open circuit failures at hot dwell temperatures that recovered at room temperature. Transverse fracture occurred at the mid-span of each resistor, running parallel to the terminations. The two resistors were installed in similar locations near the edge of the boards on two identical boards. Cracks in failed resistors were along the short axis of the resistor due to apparent bending of the resistors, Figure 1. Resistors showed no signs of pre-existing defects.

Causal Relationships Initial theories pointed to vibration-induced damage of potentially defective resistors since both resistors came from the same production lot. However, the resistor lot not only meets the requirements of procurement specification MIL-PRF-55342 but additional tests were performed and did not reveal any direct evidence of a defective resistor lot. There was no evidence of an elevated risk of defective resistors within the production lot.

Failure Analyses Independent failure analyses concluded that the cracked chip resistors were due to bending/tensile failures. There was no clear-cut root cause or visible defect identifying a crack initiation site. Both resistors exhibited a single, straight crack across the short axis (perpendicular to the long axis), indicating a bending/tensile failure without twisting.

The damage signatures are not consistent with cyclic fatigue, likely ruling out fatigue failure during vibration. In addition, NESC independent optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Figure 2, of both resistors did not identify any clear flaw locations for fatigue damage initiation and progression; therefore, the possibility of defective resistors as well as fatigue vibration as the root cause becomes unlikely. Cause ConclusionsNo direct root cause was identified, but contributing factors leading to increased design consideration needed for large footprint ceramic components located near the edges of a printed circuit board that can lead to stress cracks due to manufacturing or installation bow/twist of the printed circuit board include: Location of the relatively large resistors (case size 2512) next to the edge of the board with resistor’s long axis parallel to the card edge, increasing susceptibility to board flexure-induced damage. Excessive solder that extended to the top pads on the resistor terminations. Excessive bending moments or loads resulting from board bow/twist. Hard mounting the board to a rigid frame, which can store and amplify these bow/twist stresses. Suboptimal fastener torquing patterns, which may concentrate mounting stresses specifically at the resistor locations. Guidelines for Assembly of Ceramic Body Components to Printed Circuit BoardsThe following guidelines are to be considered given the recent experience. Component Orientation: Avoid orienting the long axis of large footprint ceramic components parallel to nearby printed circuit board edges to reduce susceptibility to global and local flexure damage. Finite Element Analysis: Perform sufficient Finite Element Analysis to demonstrate adequate stress and displacement margins on large components when they must be placed near the edge of the board. Solder Joint Fillet Limits: Keep solder off the top surface of terminations. Solder on top creates a rigid joint that transfers printed circuit board flexure directly into the ceramic increasing risk of flexure-induced cracking. Consult the individual parts manufacturers for guidance, as they may place specific limits on solder fillet height. Solder Joint Inspection: Inspect physical solder joints or review photographic images of the joints to verify that components have sufficient, but not excessive, solder fillets according to manufacturer limits. Functional Thermal Shock Testing: Perform one to three thermal cycles, including a hot-dwell functional test, prior to vibration testing, to document as built component integrity. References1. MIL-PRF-55342 Resistor, Chip, Fixed, Film, Nonestablished Reliability, Established Reliability, Space Level2. MIL-PRF-55342/9 Resistor, Fixed, Film, Chip, Nonestablished Reliability, Established Reliability, Space Level, Style RM25123. MIL-STD-202 Method 218 Board Flex

Arrow the fearless black bear doesn’t care if a foe is bigger

📅 2026-11-03  |  Read Source →

Published Nov 3, 2026 10:31 AM EST

If you are of a certain age, you might remember an innocent time when the honey badger (Mellivora capensis) took over the internet. Viral videos showing the feisty mammals that “don’t care” and punching above their weight made the honey badger a poster species for fearlessness.

That same spirit appears to be alive and well in a bear named Arrow. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded the black bear (Ursus americanus) with the 2026 Honey Badger Award.

Arrow is designated by a scar on his ear, and a thin white bit of fur by his nose that resembles a mustache. According to the rangers, Arrow has also always been a fearless bear. He suffered an injury to his back left leg during a fight with a black bear named Tatonka in 2019. He still walks with a limp, but that has not dampened his resolve.

“This year, Arrow challenged and backed down two different brown bears,” the rangers write. “Usually, brown bears are dominant over black bears due to the significant size disparity. But there are so many fish to be had at Anan Creek, the bigger bears frequently choose avoidance over violence.”

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The large area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their chunky counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here exhibits their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted here, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics and behaviors.
